clips.title: How to reduce system noise up to 98%
clips.why: PagerDuty explains the problem of an alert storm from the side of the person who gets paged: one failure underneath, many alerts on top, and a tired human in the middle.
look: Many alerts often share one cause, and the goal is one incident for one cause, not one page per alert.
Noise has a cost even when each single alert is correct: people stop reacting.
clips.after: Incident mode is our version: seven new fingerprints from one runner image become one flag, one page and one post in #ai-agents-alerts.

clips.title: The Circuit Breaker Pattern | Resilient Microservices
clips.why: The circuit breaker is a classic pattern from service design, and this short explanation covers all of its states in under four minutes.
look: Requests that are sure to fail only waste resources, so the breaker stops sending them. Our fixers would only waste VMs on a broken runner image.
The breaker opens when failures pass a threshold, and stays open for a while.
In the half-open state it tries again carefully. Our parked runs do the same after Resume: each checks that main is still red before claiming a VM.
clips.after: We use the pattern twice: incident mode for all fixers at once, and a smaller breaker that pauses one routine after 3 bad runs out of 5.

practice.q: At 11:00, five new fingerprints arrived in the last 15 minutes. A sixth arrives at 11:02. What does stormCheck return for the sixth run?

options.text: normal, because 6 is close to the limit
options.why: The rule is more than 5. Six is more than 5.

options.text: incident: it sets the paused flag, and if it is the first to set it, it pages
options.why: Six new causes in 15 minutes crosses the line. setIfAbsent decides which single caller pages.

options.text: incident, but only after the gather window ends
options.why: The gather window groups builds of one fingerprint. Storm control counts different fingerprints, and it reacts as soon as the count is over 5.

practice.q: Finish the visibility query that counts new root causes.
practice.hint: A built-in time field of every run: when it began.
practice.why: Each fixer run starts when its fingerprint first appears, so runs started in the window are the new causes in the window.

practice.q: The runner image breaks at 10:14. Put the storm in order.
items: Install steps fail in frontend, cloud and client CI, each with a different first error line
A new fixer run starts for each new fingerprint
A run's stormCheck counts more than 5 new fingerprints in 15 minutes
It sets routines:fixers:paused, pages the on-call person once and posts to #ai-agents-alerts
New fixer runs park at the gate and claim no VM
A person fixes the runner image and presses Resume; parked runs find main green and end as not_needed
practice.why: The count turns many builds into one decision, the flag turns one decision into one page, and the re-check after Resume makes sure nobody fixes a problem that is gone.

practice.q: fe-dead-code's last 5 runs ended failed, handed_off, handed_off, not_needed and rejected. Does its circuit breaker trip?

options.text: Yes, four of the five runs did not merge
options.why: Only failed and rejected count. handed_off and not_needed are not the routine's fault.

options.text: No, only 2 runs count against it
options.why: failed and rejected are two. The breaker needs three of the last five.

options.text: Yes, because two hand-offs in a row mean the routine is confused
options.why: A hand-off usually means the environment was the problem. Punishing the routine for it would pause good routines during every outage.

practice.q: Name the search attribute that routineRun sets when a run ends, and that the circuit breaker reads.
practice.before: The breaker reads each finished run's
practice.after: : merged, closed, rejected, failed, handed_off or not_needed.
practice.why: RoutineOutcome is a keyword search attribute, so the breaker can read the last runs' results with one visibility list.
